claims.text: Advanced-free-energy-sampling-guided processing will enable large-scale reactive synthesis of a RHEA–Cu composite.
The resulting RHEA–Cu composite will have a uniform and stable microstructure.
Cu and the refractory elements have an intrinsically positive heat of mixing.
A high positive mixing enthalpy causes the RHEA powder and Cu components to segregate.
Reactive consolidation, such as spark plasma sintering, can be used to synthesize the RHEA–Cu composite.
Advanced free energy sampling can optimize the temperature ramp, dwell time, and cooling rate by adjusting thermodynamic and kinetic profiles.
Rapid high-temperature processing permits reaction and consolidation while limiting Cu segregation.
RHEAs are relevant to high-temperature and advanced-nuclear-reactor environments.
The proposed process can be scalable and compatible with high-temperature, irradiation, and corrosion environments in next-generation nuclear reactors.
Free-energy-sampling-guided adjustment of reaction kinetics and interfacial diffusion barriers establishes a transient sintering microstructure that minimizes Cu segregation.
Free energy landscape exploration can identify a narrow processing window in which enhanced kinetic mixing counteracts the thermodynamic drive toward segregation.
The controlled reaction produces a homogeneous RHEA–Cu composite despite the positive heat of mixing.
The optimized process will produce a uniform, interpenetrating RHEA–Cu microstructure with greater stability and less Cu segregation than conventional processing.
Standard melting, casting, or powder-metallurgy routes cause significant Cu segregation and unstable microstructures in RHEA–Cu composites.
The method's effectiveness depends on accurately balancing reaction kinetics against thermodynamic driving forces.
Scale-up problems or unanticipated kinetic barriers could prevent effectiveness in industrial processing.
The degree of Cu-segregation reduction and improvement in microstructural uniformity is not yet known.

The hypothesis is falsified if optimized samples fail to show a statistically significant reduction in Cu segregation or improved microstructural uniformity relative to conventionally processed controls, or if unexpected phase separation occurs.
